course.title: Number Theory
course.description: The mathematics of the integers themselves — divisibility, primes, congruences, and the deep structure of arithmetic mod n that quietly powers modern cryptography. Structure adapted from MIT OpenCourseWare 18.781 Theory of Numbers (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: We say a divides b (written a | b) when…
options: b = a*k for some integer k
a and b share no common factor
questions.explanation: Divisibility means b is an exact integer multiple of a: b = a*k. See 'Divisibility and the Euclidean algorithm'.

questions.prompt: The greatest common divisor gcd(24, 36) is…
questions.explanation: The largest integer dividing both 24 and 36 is 12.

questions.prompt: A prime number is a whole number greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are…
questions.explanation: By definition a prime p > 1 has exactly two positive divisors, 1 and p.

questions.prompt: 17 mod 5 equals…
questions.explanation: 17 = 3*5 + 2, so the remainder is 2.

questions.prompt: Two integers a and b are called coprime (relatively prime) when…
questions.explanation: Coprime means their only common positive divisor is 1, i.e. gcd(a,b) = 1.

questions.prompt: The statement 'a is congruent to b (mod n)' means…
options: a + b is a multiple of n
questions.explanation: Congruence mod n means n | (a - b): a and b leave the same remainder mod n.

questions.prompt: How many primes are there?
questions.explanation: Euclid proved there are infinitely many primes — you can always build a new one.

questions.prompt: If p is prime and p divides a*b, then…
options: p divides a or p divides b
p divides both a and b
questions.explanation: This is Euclid's lemma, the key fact behind unique factorization.

lessons.title: Divisibility, the Euclidean algorithm, and linear Diophantine equations
lessons.grammar_note: In this course gcd(a,b) is always taken as a positive integer, and gcd(a,0) = a for a > 0.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Test divisibility, run the Euclidean algorithm to find gcd(a,b), reverse it to write the gcd as a combination of a and b (Bezout's identity), and use that to solve linear Diophantine equations. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what does a | b mean in one equation?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: We say a divides b, written a | b, when b = a*k for some integer k. The greatest common divisor gcd(a,b) is the largest positive integer dividing both. Euclid's algorithm computes it fast using the fact that gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a mod b): keep replacing the pair (a,b) with (b, a mod b) until the remainder is 0, and the last nonzero remainder is the gcd. Running the steps backward gives Bezout's identity: there are integers x and y with a*x + b*y = gcd(a,b). A linear Diophantine equation a*x + b*y = c asks for integer solutions x, y; it has a solution exactly when gcd(a,b) divides c, and Bezout's identity hands you one.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Euclid on gcd(48,18): 48 mod 18 = 12; 18 mod 12 = 6; 12 mod 6 = 0, so gcd = 6. Reverse it for Bezout: 6 = 18 - 12, and 12 = 48 - 2*18, so 6 = 18 - (48 - 2*18) = 3*18 - 1*48. Check: 3*18 - 48 = 54 - 48 = 6, correct, so x = -1, y = 3 solves 48*x + 18*y = 6. Solving a Diophantine equation, 6*x + 4*y = 20: gcd(6,4) = 2, and 2 divides 20, so solutions exist. One is x = 2, y = 2 (12 + 8 = 20). Another, 6*x + 4*y = 5: gcd(6,4) = 2 does not divide 5, so there are no integer solutions at all.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Find gcd(1071, 462) by Euclid. 2) Does 15 | 90? 3) Write gcd(12,8) as 12*x + 8*y. 4) Does 9*x + 6*y = 4 have integer solutions? 5) Find one integer solution of 7*x + 5*y = 1. Answers: 1) 1071 mod 462 = 147; 462 mod 147 = 21; 147 mod 21 = 0, so gcd = 21. 2) Yes, 90 = 15*6. 3) gcd = 4; 8 = 12 - 4 gives 4 = 12 - 8, so x = 1, y = -1. 4) gcd(9,6) = 3 does not divide 4, so no. 5) gcd(7,5) = 1; 7 - 5 = 2, 5 - 2*2 = 1 so 1 = 5 - 2*(7-5) = 3*5 - 2*7, giving x = -2, y = 3.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading off the final 0 as the gcd instead of the last nonzero remainder. Mistake: trying to solve a*x + b*y = c when gcd(a,b) does not divide c — no solution can exist. Exit: (a) What is gcd(100, 8)? (b) When does a*x + b*y = c have integer solutions? Answers: 100 mod 8 = 4, 8 mod 4 = 0, so gcd = 4; exactly when gcd(a,b) divides c.

lessons.title: Primes and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
lessons.grammar_note: The number 1 is neither prime nor composite — treating it as prime would break unique factorization.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Identify primes, factor an integer into primes, use factorizations to compute gcd and lcm, and explain why the primes never run out. Warm-up: list every prime below 20.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A prime is an integer p > 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and p; every other integer above 1 is composite. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says every integer greater than 1 factors into primes in exactly one way, apart from the order of the factors. This uniqueness rests on Euclid's lemma: if a prime p divides a product a*b, then p divides a or p divides b. Once you have the prime factorizations of two numbers, gcd is the product of the shared prime powers taken to the smaller exponent, and lcm takes the larger exponent. Euclid also proved there are infinitely many primes: given any finite list, multiply them all and add 1; the result is divisible by none of them, so a new prime must exist.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Factor 360: 360 = 2^3 * 3^2 * 5. Factor 84: 84 = 2^2 * 3 * 7. Their gcd uses the smaller exponent on each shared prime: gcd = 2^2 * 3 = 12. Their lcm uses the larger exponent across all primes present: lcm = 2^3 * 3^2 * 5 * 7 = 2520. Note gcd * lcm = 12 * 2520 = 30240 = 360 * 84, a handy check. Euclid's infinitude argument on the list 2, 3, 5: form 2*3*5 + 1 = 31, which is prime and not on the list — so no finite list can be complete.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Give the prime factorization of 100. 2) Is 91 prime? 3) Compute gcd(2^3*3^2, 2*3^3) from the exponents. 4) Compute lcm(4, 6). 5) Using 2*3 + 1 = 7, what does Euclid's argument show? Answers: 1) 100 = 2^2 * 5^2. 2) No, 91 = 7 * 13. 3) smaller exponents: 2^1 * 3^2 = 18. 4) 4 = 2^2, 6 = 2*3, lcm = 2^2 * 3 = 12. 5) that a prime (here 7) exists outside the list {2,3}, so primes are unlimited.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: calling 1 prime, which would let you pad any factorization with extra 1s and destroy uniqueness. Mistake: taking the larger exponent for gcd — gcd uses the smaller exponent, lcm the larger. Exit: (a) What is the prime factorization of 45? (b) For shared primes, does gcd use the smaller or larger exponent? Answers: 45 = 3^2 * 5; the smaller exponent.

lessons.title: Modular arithmetic and congruences
lessons.grammar_note: a mod n denotes the remainder in the range 0 to n-1; 'a is congruent to b (mod n)' is the relation n | (a - b).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Reduce numbers mod n, add and multiply inside a modulus, and use fast exponentiation to compute a^k mod n without huge intermediate numbers. Warm-up: on a 12-hour clock, what time is 5 hours after 10 o'clock?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: For a positive n, a mod n is the remainder when a is divided by n, always in the range 0 to n-1. We write a is congruent to b (mod n) when n divides a - b, meaning they land on the same clock position. Congruence respects addition and multiplication: if a is congruent to a' and b to b' (mod n), then a+b is congruent to a'+b' and a*b to a'*b'. So you may reduce mod n at any step, which keeps numbers small. To compute a large power a^k mod n, use repeated squaring: square your way up (a^2, a^4, a^8, ...) reducing mod n each time, and multiply together the pieces matching the binary digits of k.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: 17 mod 5 = 2, since 17 = 3*5 + 2. On a 12-hour clock 10 + 5 = 15 is congruent to 3 (mod 12). Reducing a product early: (7*8) mod 5 = 56 mod 5, but faster is (7 mod 5)*(8 mod 5) = 2*3 = 6, which is 1 (mod 5). Fast exponentiation for 3^13 mod 7: 3^1 = 3; 3^2 = 9 = 2; 3^4 = 2^2 = 4; 3^8 = 4^2 = 16 = 2 (all mod 7). Since 13 = 8 + 4 + 1, 3^13 = 3^8 * 3^4 * 3^1 = 2*4*3 = 24 = 3 (mod 7).

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Compute 100 mod 7. 2) Compute (9 + 8) mod 12. 3) Compute (6*6) mod 7. 4) Is 91 congruent to 1 (mod 9)? 5) Compute 2^10 mod 11. Answers: 1) 100 = 14*7 + 2, so 2. 2) 17 mod 12 = 5. 3) 36 mod 7 = 1. 4) 91 = 10*9 + 1, so yes, congruent to 1. 5) 2^5 = 32 = 10 (mod 11), so 2^10 = 10^2 = 100 = 1 (mod 11).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reporting a negative remainder — in this convention a mod n lives in 0 to n-1, so -1 mod 5 is 4, not -1. Mistake: computing a^k as a giant integer first; reduce mod n at every squaring instead. Exit: (a) What is -1 mod 7? (b) What is (4*4*4) mod 5? Answers: 6, since -1 + 7 = 6; 64 mod 5 = 4.

questions.prompt: Using Euclid's algorithm, gcd(48, 18) equals…
The linear equation 6*x + 4*y = 5 has how many integer solutions?
questions.explanation: gcd(6,4) = 2 does not divide 5, so no integer solution exists.

questions.prompt: The prime factorization of 360 is…
For gcd(2^3 * 3^2, 2 * 3^3), taking the smaller exponent on each shared prime gives…
questions.explanation: Smaller exponents: 2^1 * 3^2 = 2 * 9 = 18.

questions.prompt: Reducing modulo 5, the product (7*8) mod 5 equals…
questions.explanation: 56 mod 5 = 1, or faster 2*3 = 6 = 1 (mod 5).

questions.prompt: The value of -1 mod 7 in the range 0 to 6 is…
questions.explanation: Add 7 to -1 to land in range: -1 + 7 = 6.

lessons.title: Linear congruences and the Chinese Remainder Theorem
lessons.grammar_note: The congruence a*x is congruent to b (mod n) is solvable exactly when gcd(a,n) divides b; when gcd(a,n) = 1 the solution is unique mod n.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Solve a single linear congruence, find a modular inverse, and combine several congruences with different moduli using the Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT). Warm-up: what is the inverse of 3 mod 7 — that is, which x makes 3*x congruent to 1 (mod 7)?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A linear congruence a*x is congruent to b (mod n) has a solution exactly when gcd(a,n) divides b. When gcd(a,n) = 1, a has a modular inverse a^(-1) — the unique value mod n with a*a^(-1) congruent to 1 — which you find from Bezout's identity, and then x is congruent to a^(-1) * b (mod n). The Chinese Remainder Theorem handles several congruences at once: if the moduli are pairwise coprime, then a system such as x congruent to r1 (mod n1) and x congruent to r2 (mod n2) has exactly one solution modulo the product n1*n2. You build it by stitching the pieces together with the inverses of each partial product.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Inverse of 3 mod 7: Bezout gives 3*5 = 15 = 1 (mod 7), so 3^(-1) = 5. Solve 3*x congruent to 4 (mod 7): x = 5*4 = 20 = 6 (mod 7); check 3*6 = 18 = 4 (mod 7), correct. CRT on x congruent to 2 (mod 3) and x congruent to 3 (mod 5): moduli 3 and 5 are coprime, product 15. Test values congruent to 3 (mod 5): 3, 8, 13; of these 8 is congruent to 2 (mod 3), so x congruent to 8 (mod 15). Check: 8 = 2*3 + 2 and 8 = 1*5 + 3, both correct. A non-example: 2*x congruent to 3 (mod 4) has no solution, because gcd(2,4) = 2 does not divide 3.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Find the inverse of 4 mod 9. 2) Solve 5*x congruent to 3 (mod 11). 3) Does 6*x congruent to 4 (mod 9) have a solution? 4) Solve the system x congruent to 1 (mod 4), x congruent to 2 (mod 5). 5) What is the unique modulus of that combined solution? Answers: 1) 4*7 = 28 = 1 (mod 9), so 7. 2) 5^(-1) mod 11 is 9 (since 5*9 = 45 = 1), so x = 9*3 = 27 = 5 (mod 11). 3) gcd(6,9) = 3 does not divide 4, so no. 4) values congruent to 2 (mod 5): 2, 7, 12, 17; 17 is congruent to 1 (mod 4), so x congruent to 17 (mod 20). 5) 4*5 = 20.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: dividing both sides of a congruence by a number that shares a factor with n — you may only divide by something coprime to n. Mistake: applying CRT when the moduli are not coprime; the clean unique-solution statement needs pairwise coprime moduli. Exit: (a) What is the inverse of 2 mod 5? (b) Over what modulus is a CRT solution unique for moduli 3 and 7? Answers: 3, since 2*3 = 6 = 1 (mod 5); modulo 21.

lessons.title: Fermat's little theorem, Euler's totient, and primitive roots
lessons.grammar_note: Fermat's little theorem needs p prime and gcd(a,p) = 1; Euler's theorem generalizes it to any modulus n with gcd(a,n) = 1.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Apply Fermat's little theorem and Euler's theorem to shrink exponents, compute Euler's totient phi(n), and recognize what a primitive root is. Warm-up: without multiplying it out, what should 2^6 be mod 7?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Fermat's little theorem: if p is prime and p does not divide a, then a^(p-1) is congruent to 1 (mod p). Euler's totient phi(n) counts the integers from 1 to n that are coprime to n; for a prime p, phi(p) = p - 1, and for a prime power, phi(p^k) = p^k - p^(k-1). Because phi is multiplicative over coprime factors, phi(m*n) = phi(m)*phi(n) when gcd(m,n) = 1. Euler's theorem generalizes Fermat: if gcd(a,n) = 1, then a^phi(n) is congruent to 1 (mod n). This is exactly what lets you reduce a huge exponent modulo phi(n). A primitive root mod n is a value g whose powers g^1, g^2, ... cycle through every residue coprime to n before repeating; its order is phi(n), and primitive roots exist for moduli like primes.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Fermat: 2^6 mod 7 = 1, since 7 is prime and 2^(7-1) is congruent to 1. Use it to reduce 2^100 mod 7: 100 = 6*16 + 4, so 2^100 = (2^6)^16 * 2^4 congruent to 1 * 16 = 2 (mod 7). Totients: phi(10) = phi(2)*phi(5) = 1*4 = 4 (the coprime residues are 1, 3, 7, 9); phi(9) = 9 - 3 = 6. Euler: 3^phi(10) = 3^4 = 81 = 1 (mod 10), matching. Primitive root: 3 is a primitive root mod 7, because its powers 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1 (mod 7) run through all six nonzero residues before returning to 1.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Compute 5^6 mod 7 using Fermat. 2) Compute phi(12). 3) Reduce 2^50 mod 7. 4) What is phi(p) for a prime p? 5) Is 2 a primitive root mod 5? Answers: 1) 7 is prime and does not divide 5, so 5^6 is congruent to 1 (mod 7). 2) 12 = 2^2 * 3, phi = (4-2)*(3-1) = 2*2 = 4. 3) 50 = 6*8 + 2, so 2^50 congruent to 2^2 = 4 (mod 7). 4) p - 1. 5) powers of 2 mod 5 are 2, 4, 3, 1 — all four nonzero residues, so yes.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: applying Fermat when p divides a or n is not prime — you need gcd(a,p) = 1, and for composite moduli use Euler with phi(n). Mistake: reducing the exponent mod n instead of mod phi(n); it is the exponent that lives mod phi(n). Exit: (a) What is phi(8)? (b) What is 4^phi(9) mod 9? Answers: phi(8) = 8 - 4 = 4; since gcd(4,9) = 1, Euler gives 4^6 congruent to 1 (mod 9).

questions.prompt: The modular inverse of 3 mod 7 is…
questions.explanation: 3 * 5 = 15 is congruent to 1 (mod 7), so the inverse is 5.

questions.prompt: The system x congruent to 2 (mod 3) and x congruent to 3 (mod 5) has solution…
questions.explanation: 8 = 2*3 + 2 and 8 = 1*5 + 3; the moduli are coprime so the answer is unique mod 15.

questions.prompt: By Fermat's little theorem, for a prime p and a not divisible by p, a^(p-1) is congruent to…
questions.explanation: That is the statement of Fermat's little theorem.

questions.prompt: Euler's totient phi(10) equals…
questions.explanation: The residues coprime to 10 are 1, 3, 7, 9 — four of them.

questions.prompt: Using Fermat, 2^100 mod 7 equals…
questions.explanation: 2^6 is congruent to 1 (mod 7) and 100 = 6*16 + 4, so 2^100 congruent to 2^4 = 16 = 2 (mod 7).

questions.prompt: A primitive root g modulo n has multiplicative order equal to…
questions.explanation: Its powers cycle through all phi(n) residues coprime to n, so its order is phi(n).

lessons.title: Quadratic residues and an application: RSA public-key basics
lessons.grammar_note: RSA's decryption works because of Euler's theorem: choosing d with e*d congruent to 1 (mod phi(n)) inverts the exponentiation.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Decide whether a number is a quadratic residue mod p, and walk through how RSA public-key encryption sets up keys, encrypts, and decrypts using Euler's theorem. Warm-up: which nonzero values mod 7 are perfect squares?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A quadratic residue mod p is a nonzero value that equals some square x^2 (mod p); the others are nonresidues. For an odd prime p exactly (p-1)/2 of the nonzero residues are squares, because x and -x give the same square and pair the residues up. Quadratic residues are one window into the deep multiplicative structure mod p; RSA public-key cryptography is a dramatic application of that structure. RSA works like this: pick two large primes p and q and set n = p*q, so phi(n) = (p-1)*(q-1). Choose a public exponent e coprime to phi(n), and compute the private exponent d with e*d congruent to 1 (mod phi(n)) using the modular inverse. The public key is (n, e); the private key is d. To encrypt a message m, compute c = m^e mod n. To decrypt, compute c^d mod n, which returns m because m^(e*d) = m^(1 + k*phi(n)) is congruent to m (mod n) by Euler's theorem. Security rests on the difficulty of factoring n back into p and q without the private key.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Quadratic residues mod 7: squaring 1..6 gives 1, 4, 2, 2, 4, 1, so the residues are {1, 2, 4} — exactly (7-1)/2 = 3 of them — and {3, 5, 6} are nonresidues. A tiny RSA run with p = 3, q = 11: n = 33, phi(n) = 2*10 = 20. Pick e = 7, coprime to 20; its inverse d satisfies 7*d congruent to 1 (mod 20), and d = 3 works since 7*3 = 21 = 1 (mod 20). Encrypt m = 2: c = 2^7 mod 33 = 128 mod 33 = 29. Decrypt: 29^3 mod 33. Compute 29 congruent to -4 (mod 33), so 29^3 congruent to (-4)^3 = -64 = -64 + 66 = 2 (mod 33) — the original message returns.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) List the quadratic residues mod 5. 2) How many nonzero quadratic residues does an odd prime p have? 3) With p = 5, q = 7, what are n and phi(n)? 4) If e = 5 and phi(n) = 24, find d with e*d congruent to 1 (mod 24). 5) In RSA, why can the decryptor recover m? Answers: 1) squares of 1..4 are 1, 4, 4, 1, so {1, 4}. 2) (p-1)/2. 3) n = 35, phi(n) = 4*6 = 24. 4) 5*5 = 25 = 1 (mod 24), so d = 5. 5) because m^(e*d) is congruent to m (mod n) by Euler's theorem, since e*d is congruent to 1 (mod phi(n)).

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: choosing a public exponent e that shares a factor with phi(n) — then no inverse d exists and decryption breaks. Mistake: thinking RSA hides messages by secrecy of the method; it is the hardness of factoring n and of finding phi(n) that protects the private key. Exit: (a) How many nonzero quadratic residues are there mod 11? (b) In RSA, what equation must the private exponent d satisfy? Answers: (11-1)/2 = 5; e*d congruent to 1 (mod phi(n)).

questions.prompt: gcd(1071, 462) computed by the Euclidean algorithm is…
Which equation has NO integer solutions?
questions.explanation: gcd(9,6) = 3 does not divide 4; the others all have their gcd dividing the right side.

questions.prompt: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic guarantees that every integer above 1…
options: factors into primes in exactly one way up to order
has an even number of divisors
is a product of two primes
questions.explanation: Unique factorization into primes is the theorem's content.

questions.prompt: lcm(4, 6) equals…
questions.explanation: 4 = 2^2, 6 = 2*3, so lcm takes the larger exponents: 2^2 * 3 = 12.

questions.prompt: The value 3^13 mod 7 is…
questions.explanation: 3^6 is congruent to 1 (mod 7) by Fermat; 13 = 6*2 + 1, so 3^13 congruent to 3^1 = 3.

questions.prompt: The modular inverse of 5 mod 11 is…
questions.explanation: 5 * 9 = 45 is congruent to 1 (mod 11).

questions.prompt: The system x congruent to 1 (mod 4), x congruent to 2 (mod 5) is solved by…
questions.explanation: 17 = 4*4 + 1 and 17 = 3*5 + 2; moduli 4 and 5 are coprime so it is unique mod 20.

questions.prompt: Euler's totient phi(12) equals…
Euler's theorem says that if gcd(a,n) = 1 then…
questions.explanation: a raised to phi(n) returns to 1 modulo n — the generalization of Fermat.

questions.prompt: The nonzero quadratic residues mod 7 are…
questions.explanation: Squaring 1..6 mod 7 yields 1, 4, 2, 2, 4, 1, so the residues are {1, 2, 4}.

questions.prompt: In RSA with public exponent e, the private exponent d must satisfy…
questions.explanation: d is the inverse of e modulo phi(n); this is what makes decryption invert encryption.

questions.prompt: RSA's practical security rests mainly on the difficulty of…
options: factoring the modulus n into its two primes
questions.explanation: Knowing p and q reveals phi(n) and hence d; factoring large n is the hard problem.
